title: TF drift detection & partial-apply recovery smoke runbook
body:
Purpose:
This runbook is a compact, pragmatic playbook for detecting Terraform drift and recovering from partial/failed applies in Private Deployments (VPC / on-prem). Focus is on quick triage, non-destructive verification, and a safe path to either complete apply or roll back to a known good state.

Scope:
- Applies to the private-deployments Terraform codebase and customer TF modules (network, bootstrap, runtime, access controls).
- Assumes S3/remote backend with state locking or similar.
- Target audience: SREs / infra engineers on first response rotation.

When to use:
- An apply crashed midway (timeouts, provider errors, OOM in bootstrap).
- Customer reports partial networking / some nodes unhealthy after an upgrade.
- terraform plan shows inexplicable differences vs what’s running.

Quick triage checklist (5–10 minutes):
1) Confirm symptom: slack #pd-instances / customer ticket, timestamp, and last terraform apply commit.
2) Check CI / CD job logs: which step failed? capture apply output.
3) Check backend state lock: is there a current lock? (S3/DynamoDB/GCS).
   - Command: aws s3api get-object --bucket <bucket> --key <state-lock-key> (or check dynamodb)
4) Run terraform workspace/vars sanity: echo workspace, check TF_VAR_ envs.
5) Run quick health probes: ping API endpoint, check kube nodes (kubectl get nodes -A), nvidia-smi on GPU hosts if available.

Detecting drift vs partial apply:
- Drift (external change): terraform plan --detailed-exitcode after terraform refresh will return 2 if differences exist.
  Commands: 
    terraform init -backend-config=...
    terraform refresh
    terraform plan -detailed-exitcode -out=plan.tfout || true
- Partial apply (apply failed mid-run): state has some resources created but accompanying resources/outputs missing; apply log shows error near the end.
  Clues: some cloud resources exist (instances, subnets) but state lacks expected refs, or state has resources without corresponding cloud resources (orphaned).
  Commands:
    terraform state list > state.list
    terraform state show <resource>
    aws ec2 describe-instances --filters "Name=tag:Name,Values=<name>"

Non-destructive verification (before any apply):
- Compare resource counts: terraform state list | wc -l vs inventory scripts.
- For critical modules (network, lb, bootstrap hosts): verify actual cloud objects exist (subnets, route tables, security groups).
- Check bootstrap logs on nodes (/var/log/redwood-bootstrap.log) for config errors.

Recovery strategies (ordered by safety):
A) Resume/complete the apply (preferred if apply failed due to transient provider errors)
  - Ensure state lock is cleared (if locked, identify locker and wait 5–10 min; do not force-unlock without coordination).
  - Re-run terraform apply with the same variables/commit. Use small timeout and watch: terraform apply "plan.tfout" or terraform apply -auto-approve.
  - If plan still proposes destructive changes, pause and review.

B) Taint specific resource + reapply (when one resource is broken)
  - Identify broken resource (e.g., aws_instance.runtime-0).
  - Command: terraform taint <resource> OR terraform state rm <resource> then re-import if needed.
  - Reapply targeted module: cd modules/runtime && terraform apply -target=module.runtime -auto-approve

C) Import an out-of-band resource (when infra was created manually or by a failed script)
  - Find resource identifiers from cloud (instance id, subnet id).
  - Command: terraform import module.runtime.aws_instance.runtime[0] i-0123456789abcdef
  - After import, terraform plan should be clean or show the minimal changes.

D) State surgery (last resort)
  - Snapshot the backend state first (copy S3 object, export state file).
  - Use terraform state rm / mv to prune inconsistent entries.
  - Use terraform import to reconstitute resources. Document every command and notify on-call.

Partial-apply specific recovery flow (detailed):
1) Capture current state & logs (mandatory)
   - aws s3 cp s3://<state-bucket>/<state-key> ./state-backup-<ts>.backup
   - Save CI job logs to GH gist or ticket.
2) Lock state (if backend supports explicit lock) or announce in Slack channel to prevent concurrent applies.
3) Identify boundary of partial changes: which modules completed, which failed. Look at apply log and search for "Apply complete" markers and error stack.
4) For modules that completed but missing outputs (e.g., autoscaling group created but ASG tags not applied), run targeted apply on that module only: terraform apply -target=module.<name> -auto-approve
5) For resources created outside TF (or created by earlier failed scripts), import into state instead of recreating.
6) Validate downstream dependencies (eg. LB target groups, instance registration).
7) Run post-recovery smoke tests (see below).

Smoke tests (post-fix, quick wins):
- Network: traceroute from customer gateway to control-plane endpoint; verify route tables include correct CIDRs.
- API: curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer <test-token>" https://<api>/healthz -> expect 200 and JSON {"ok":true}
- Console: hit single sign-on endpoint, ensure login flow returns status 302 -> console
- Agents/runtime: ssh into runtime node, check redwood processes: ps aux | egrep "redwood|runtime" and tail last 200 lines of logs.
- GPU: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,utilization.gpu,driver_version --format=csv,noheader
- KV/cache: send a short sequence of requests that should hit cache (prefix key checks), verify response latencies drop.

Common error fingerprints and focused remediations:
- Provider rate limits during apply: Retry with backoff, split apply into smaller modules, set provider parallelism via TF_VAR or -parallelism flag.
- State lock persisted (DynamoDB stuck): identify locker (DynamoDB record), check CI job owner, if CI job died, force-unlock after confirmation: terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID>
- DNS records not created: check credentials used in apply (IAM permissions), then reapply module providing TTL/zone.
- Bootstrap script OOM/crashloops: capture /var/log/redwood-bootstrap.log, check systemd unit, increase systemd StartLimitBurst or resource limits, re-run bootstrap script manually.
- Partial network (subnet exists but route table missing): terraform state show aws_subnet.<x> and aws_route_table.<y>; if route missing, reapply network module.

Verification commands (copy/paste):
- terraform init -backend-config=...
- terraform refresh
- terraform plan -detailed-exitcode -out=plan.tfout || true
- terraform state list | sed -n '1,200p'
- terraform state show module.bootstrap.aws_instance.bootstrap[0]
- aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-ids i-... --query 'Reservations[*].Instances[*].[InstanceId,State.Name,Tags]'
- kubectl get pods -A --selector=app=redwood -o wide

Rollback plan (if recovery risks more damage):
1) Identify last known-good commit/tag in the terraform repo (CI artifacts or tags).
2) Check out that commit locally, run terraform init and plan against remote backend (don’t apply yet).
3) Run terraform plan and verify it converges to fewer/different changes; share plan with stake-holders.
4) If approved, apply on a maintenance window with a runbook owner and two-step approval.

Escalation & data to collect before paging ENG-ONCALL:
- Full terraform apply log, workspace, and commit hash.
- State snapshot (S3 path), terraform state list and show for a handful of critical resources.
- Node-level logs (/var/log/*, kubelet logs).
- nvidia-smi output (if GPU related).
- Timing of when the CI job ran vs when resources were created.
- Customer impact summary (latency, errors, endpoints affected).

Playbook hygiene / runbook notes (notes to self):
- Always create a state snapshot before manual state edits.
- Prefer imports over delete/recreate for customer resources.
- Document every manual change in the ticket (commands run, who approved).
- Add small automation: a script that runs terraform plan -detailed-exitcode and uploads plan output to ticket automatically.

Unresolved questions & follow-ups:
- Should we add a transient-apply-safe-mode in CI that splits large applies into per-module steps? (INF-2345 follow-up)
- Can we add provider rate-limit backoff plugin globally?
- Consider adding a lightweight drift-monitor that runs weekly and alerts on unexpected changes.

Appendix: useful snippets and helpers
- Extract last apply block from the CI logs: awk '/Apply complete/,/module\./{print}' ci-apply.log | tail -n 200
- Snapshot state to local: aws s3 cp s3://<bucket>/<key> ./state-<ts>.json
- Quick import example: terraform import module.runtime.aws_instance.runtime[0] i-0abc123def456

Contact & channels:
- Slack: #private-deploy-first-response, #pd-oncall
- Pager: ENG-ONCALL (if major outage)
- Owners: eng-private-deployments rotation (see team calendar)

---
Checklist (tick off during incident):
[ ] capture state snapshot
[ ] collect CI job logs + apply stderr
[ ] confirm state lock status
[ ] run terraform refresh and plan
[ ] target-apply safe modules first
[ ] import resources instead of re-creating when possible
[ ] run post-fix smoke tests (network, API, GPUs, bootstrap logs)
[ ] document actions in ticket and notify customer with ETA

This doc is intentionally concise — use it as an incident accelerant, not a replacement for deep debugging. Add any extra remediation steps discovered back into this file in the ticket for future runs.
